summary.title: Mechanochemical synthesis of eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell (calcite) and KH2PO4
summary.authors: Roger Borges; Amanda Soares Giroto; Rodrigo Klaic; Fernando Wypych; Caue Ribeiro
summary.executive_summary: This study presents a solvent-free mechanochemical method for synthesizing eco-friendly potassium calcium phosphate fertilizers from eggshell waste (calcite) and monobasic potassium dihydrogen phosphate (KH2PO4). The process utilizes high-energy ball milling to promote solid-state reactions, resulting in the formation of K3CaH(PO4)2 and potentially CaKPO4 phases. The primary objective is to create a 'smart release' fertilizer that improves nutrient management by delaying the bioavailability of phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) while enhancing the bioavailability of calcium (Ca) in acidic soils. Experimental results demonstrate that milling for 2 hours at 600 rpm yields optimal phase formation. In citric acid solution, the milled samples exhibited slower release kinetics for P and K compared to the KH2PO4 precursor, fitting pseudo-second-order models. Conversely, calcium release was significantly faster than from raw eggshell. Soil release assays confirmed these trends, with the milled sample showing a progressive P release (45 mg/kg at 30 days) compared to the rapid release of KH2PO4 (107 mg/kg at 3 days). Furthermore, the formation of hydroxyapatite in soil conditions was identified as a mechanism for long-term P and Ca retention. The P radial diffusion of the milled sample was intermediate, 34% faster than struvite but 22% slower than KH2PO4. This approach leverages reverse logistics to convert food industry waste into a valuable agricultural input, offering a sustainable alternative to conventional fertilizers with improved nutrient efficiency and reduced environmental impact.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents a solvent-free mechanochemical method for synthesizing eco-friendly potassium calcium phosphate fertilizers from eggshell waste (calcite) and monobasic potassium dihydrogen phosphate (KH2PO4). The process utilizes high-energy ball milling to promote solid-state reactions, resulting in the formation of K3CaH(PO4)2 and potentially CaKPO4 phases. The primary objective is to create a 'smart release' fertilizer that improves nutrient management by delaying the bioavailability of phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) while enhancing the bioavailability of calcium (Ca) in acidic soils. Experimental results demonstrate that milling for 2 hours at 600 rpm yields optimal phase formation. In citric acid solution, the milled samples exhibited slower release kinetics for P and K compared to the KH2PO4 precursor, fitting pseudo-second-order models. Conversely, calcium release was significantly faster than from raw eggshell. Soil release assays confirmed these trends, with the milled sample showing a progressive P release (45 mg/kg at 30 days) compared to the rapid release of KH2PO4 (107 mg/kg at 3 days). Furthermore, the formation of hydroxyapatite in soil conditions was identified as a mechanism for long-term P and Ca retention. The P radial diffusion of the milled sample was intermediate, 34% faster than struvite but 22% slower than KH2PO4. This approach leverages reverse logistics to convert food industry waste into a valuable agricultural input, offering a sustainable alternative to conventional fertilizers with improved nutrient efficiency and reduced environmental impact.

Research Context
Reverse logistics is applied to agriculture to reuse solid waste. Eggshells are significant food industry wastes and calcite sources. Millions of tons of eggshells are disposed in landfills. Solid-state mechanochemical activation promotes chemical reactions via mechanical energy. Previous studies used phosphoric acid solutions for hydroxyapatite synthesis. No prior mechanochemical process for K3CaH(PO4)2 from eggshell was reported.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to synthesize potassium calcium phosphates from eggshell and KH2PO4. The hypothesis is that mechanochemical activation forms new phosphate phases. The resulting materials are hypothesized to be smart release fertilizers. It is predicted that P and K bioavailability will be delayed. It is predicted that calcium bioavailability will be improved. The process is expected to be solvent-free and waste-free.

Methodological Details
Eggshells were collected, washed, and dried at room temperature. KH2PO4 was supplied by Vetec as a reagent. Milling used a Fritsch Pulverisette 7 high-energy ball mill. A 250 ml zirconia bowl with five 15 mm zirconia balls was used. The weight ratio of eggshell to KH2PO4 was 1:1. Milling times varied from 15 min to 24 h. Milling speeds varied from 100 to 600 rpm. Samples were characterized by XRD, NMR MAS, TGA, and DSC. Nutrient content was determined via acid digestion and atomic absorption. Release assays used 2 wt% citric acid solution. Pellets were standardized to 100 mg/L of P. Soil diffusion assays used 78 g of dry sieved soil. Soil release experiments used 50 g of sandy soil. Phosphorus was quantified using molybdenum blue colorimetry. Potassium and calcium were quantified by flame atomic absorption.

Procedures And Architectures
The milling process applied mechanical energy to break reagent bonds. The reaction involves CaCO3 decomposition and phosphate formation. XRD patterns were recorded from 3 to 40 degrees 2-theta. Cu Kα radiation with 0.1546 nm wavelength was used for XRD. TGA was performed under synthetic air flow of 60 mL/min. The heating rate for TGA was 10 °C per minute. NMR MAS used a 10 kHz rotation speed. The chemical shift reference for NMR was ADP. Pellets were formed using a steel pelletizer at 5 bar pressure. Release kinetics were fitted using pseudo-first and second-order models. Soil P diffusion was analyzed using GNU Image Manipulation Program. Soil samples were extracted using HCl and KCl methods.

Key Results
Milling for 2 h at 400 rpm produced K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4. No chemical reaction was observed below 2 h or 400 rpm. TGA of KH2PO4 showed residual mass of 89%. Eggshell TGA showed calcite decomposition below 700 °C. Milled samples showed three mass loss events at 280, 420, and 710 °C. Thermal treatment at 420 °C converted samples to KCaPO4. 31P NMR showed a signal at 3.74 ppm for KH2PO4. Milled samples showed NMR shifts at 3.28 and 2.82 ppm. A pyrophosphate signal was observed at -4.78 ppm. P and K release followed pseudo-second-order kinetics. Kinetic constants decreased from KH2PO4 to milled samples. KH2PO4 released 107 mg/kg P in soil after 3 days. Milled sample released 45 mg/kg P in soil after 30 days. P radial diffusion of milled sample was 1.99 cm at day 2. KH2PO4 P radial diffusion was 2.62 cm at day 2. Milled sample P diffusion was 34% faster than struvite. Milled sample P diffusion was 22% slower than KH2PO4. Bioavailable calcium increased to 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days. Hydroxyapatite formation was identified in soil conditions.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The formed phosphates act as smart release fertilizers. Mechanochemical activation enables solvent-free synthesis. Delayed P and K release improves nutrient management. Enhanced Ca bioavailability benefits acidic soils. Hydroxyapatite formation provides long-term P and Ca sources. The process aligns with green chemistry and reverse logistics.

Claims
Mechanochemical synthesis of eggshell and KH2PO4 produces K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4. XRD patterns confirmed the presence of K3CaH(PO4)2. XRD patterns indicated possible CaKPO4 formation. NMR MAS supported the formation of calcium phosphates. Some samples showed unclear phosphate phases initially. This creates a new class of phosphate fertilizers.
The milled fertilizer provides delayed release of P and K. P release was slower in milled samples than KH2PO4. Kinetic constants decreased for milled samples. Soil P release was progressive over 30 days. KH2PO4 released P much faster in soil. This improves nutrient management in soil systems.
The milled fertilizer enhances calcium bioavailability compared to raw eggshell. Calcium release was faster from milled samples. Bioavailable Ca increased to 30.97 mg/kg in soil. Raw eggshell showed no increase in bioavailable Ca. Calcium release in citric acid was still slower than KH2PO4. This provides a bioavailable Ca source for acidic soils.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Milling time and speed were varied to determine optimal conditions. Thermal treatment was used to analyze phase transitions. Comparison with struvite provided a benchmark for slow release.

Ethical Considerations
The study uses waste materials, reducing environmental impact.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows XRD patterns of milled samples. Figure 2 shows TGA curves of precursors and milled samples. Figure 3 shows XRD patterns after thermal treatment. Figure 4 shows 31P NMR MAS spectra. Figure 5 shows nutrient release kinetics in citric acid. Figure 6 shows nutrient release kinetics in soil. Figure 7 shows XRD patterns of soil residues.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a solvent-free mechanochemical synthesis of K-Ca phosphates from eggshell waste. 2. The strongest evidence is the delayed P/K release and enhanced Ca bioavailability in soil assays. 3. The future path involves using these materials as nanocomposites for faster release if needed.
